item.title: Lake James BioBlitz — Sat Sep 19, 9:00 AM — Lake James State Park
item.description:
Join the North Carolina Native Plant Society Foothills Chapter and Lake James State Park for the Lake James BioBlitz on September 19, 2026, from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m.
A BioBlitz is a community science event focused on discovering and documenting as many species as possible in a designated area. Participants will explore Lake James State Park while searching for and identifying plants, animals, fungi, insects, and other organisms that make the park their home.
The event will begin with a talk from a Lake James State Park Ranger about local ecology before participants head into the field to explore diverse habitats and search for species. Whether you are an experienced naturalist or simply curious about the natural world, all skill levels are welcome. This is a great opportunity to learn more about the biodiversity of Lake James State Park while contributing valuable observations to our collective understanding of the park's natural resources.

item.title: NC the Beautiful: Invasive Plant Purge — Sat Oct 10, 12:00 PM — Haw River State Park - Iron Ore Belt Access
item.description:
“Invasive” plants are introduced, aggressively-growing plants that negatively impact local ecosystems. Join park staff at Haw River State Park’s Iron Ore Belt Access to help remove these leafy invaders!
Typical workdays start with paperwork for new volunteers (less than five minutes) followed by a short hike to the work area where volunteers will receive instruction on how to identify the target species of the day. The rest of the time will be used on employing hands-on, seasonally appropriate techniques to remove invasive plants from the landscape, helping to restore the area for native plants and wildlife.
Advance registration is required as supplies and space are limited. This opportunity is only open to volunteers ages 12 and up. Any volunteers under the age of 16 must be registered with and accompanied by an adult.

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Sat Nov 14 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage — Sat Nov 14, 10:00 AM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Living History Museum Days at Hickory Ridge History Museum in Boone, NC — Sat Nov 14, 10:00 AM — Hickory Ridge History Museum
item.description:
We're going back to our roots.
This season, Hickory Ridge History Museum proudly reintroduces Living History Museum Days, a return to the immersive, hands-on spirit that once defined us as Hickory Ridge Living History Museum and “village”. On select days this summer, the cabins will come alive with the sights, sounds, and smells of 18th-century life in the North Carolina mountains.
From open-hearth cooking and blacksmithing to weaving, spinning, woodworking, and frontier chores, guests will experience a day in the life of the early settlers who called this region home. Our interpreters and volunteers will demonstrate traditional skills throughout the village, inviting you to explore, ask questions, and connect with the everyday stories of Appalachian history.
Whether you’re a longtime visitor or discovering us for the first time, Living History Museum Days are your chance to step deeper into the past and to be part of its future.

item.title: The History Lake James: From Native Lands to Modern Recreation — Sat Nov 14, 10:00 AM — Lake James State Park
item.description:
Join us at Lake James State Park for “The History of Lake James: From Native Lands to Modern Recreation.” This program explores the rich cultural and historical timeline of the settlement and development of Lake James, from the Indigenous tribes who first lived along the banks of the rivers, to the development of hydroelectric generation that created the lake as we know it, and finally to today’s recreational opportunities within the state park and surrounding area. It’s a great way to learn how the landscape and its uses have transformed over time while enjoying the natural beauty of Lake James.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Fri Nov 13 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.
